title: A Change We Didn't Choose
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. traces how student motivation, the subject of his decade-long research for The Will to Learn, became an acute crisis through two compounding, unchosen disruptions: the pandemic's disorienting effect on grading, testing, and expectations, followed by ChatGPT's November 2022 release and the ensuing AI arms race among tech giants. He describes educators watching techno-utopians and doomsayers argue past each other while students — especially those already disengaged — used AI as a ready workaround for schoolwork, and cites survey data suggesting nearly all secondary students with internet access have now used AI for school tasks. Rather than resolve the uncertainty, Stuart validates teachers' discomfort — naming the exhaustion of a change nobody opted into — before pivoting to reasons for hope that don't depend on answering whether AI helps or harms learning. He grounds that hope in the constancy of the work itself: growth toward mastery of real disciplines is good regardless of the technological weather, and young people remain hungry for teachers who genuinely care about that work. The piece closes as a pep talk aimed at steadying colleagues rather than prescribing any specific AI policy.
points: Stuart frames 2020s teaching as absorbing two unchosen, compounding shocks in sequence: the pandemic's disruption of grading/testing norms and then ChatGPT's late-2022 release triggering a corporate AI arms race.
He cites NVIDIA's rise from a $270 billion to a $3.3 trillion market cap as a concrete marker of how fast and how large the AI-driven economic shift became.
Survey data he cites suggests nearly all secondary students with internet access have already used AI for school-related tasks, undercutting any wait-and-see stance for teachers.
Rather than adjudicate whether AI helps or harms learning, Stuart explicitly sets that question aside and instead anchors teachers' confidence in the unchanging value of growth toward mastery.
The essay validates teacher discomfort directly ("we get to say we're not happy about it") before pivoting to reasons for hope, functioning as morale-support writing rather than policy guidance.
quotes: First, the pandemic happened. Carrots and sticks blipped out of existence, only to come back in a jittery, jagged way. College admissions tests became optional.
And then, as if we needed more, ChatGPT's November 2022 public release unleashed a phenomenon that quickly resembled a technological arms race.
We get to say, amidst this change we didn't choose, that the rate of change is a LOT and we weren't given an opt-in. We get to say we're not happy about it.
Young people are hungry for teachers like you and I who care about the work of learning and the transformative magic it works in the human soul.
The work of learning is good. It transforms the human soul. It has before and it can again.
